job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Kira Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in applied AI at Fenwick University, and I live in a student house with five others, a noisy place with a good kitchen. My day is lectures, a part-time project with a local business, and choir practice on Wednesday evenings. My parents run a dairy farm two hours away, and they cover my fees, so I have no debt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the project with the local business.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a bakery chain with four shops, and I'm building a tool that predicts how many loaves to bake each morning, using sales and the weather. I use AI assistants all day for coding and writing. My bachelor's in software engineering was only a pass, because I spent my second year working on a farm app for my parents, but I have no regrets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because then people stop worrying and get on with making useful things. At the bakery I'd say the forecasting tool is plain statistics and still saves them money. I'd probably also tell my choir friends not to believe every headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plan works: finish the master's, then join a company that builds practical tools for businesses, and keep my own projects on the side. I have over six months saved and several firms in Fenwick that hire. Nothing dramatic changes, so my steady progress is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the bakery whether they'd pay for the tool after my project ends, even a small monthly fee. I'd apply to about ten firms from March and keep working on the farm app. I'd also sign up two more bakeries from the owner's contacts, to see if it can become a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and content. It's like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the farm app matter in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a lot to me and my parents. The app tracks the herd's milk yield and flags a cow that's off her feed, and my dad uses it every day. It saved him from a vet bill last winter, which he told the whole church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you describe your attitude to risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take risks I can recover from. Putting my savings into something I don't understand isn't one of them. A side business with a part-time income is fine. My father says the same about buying cows, so it must be in the blood.

say: Good, because then people stop worrying and **make useful things**.
I'd tell my choir friends not to believe every **headline**.
think: My plan works: finish the master's and join a firm that builds **practical tools**.
Nothing dramatic changes, so steady **progress** is enough.
do: Ask the bakery to pay a small **monthly fee** for the tool after my project.
Apply to ten firms and sign up **two more bakeries**.
feel: **Calm** and content, like a quiet Sunday.
S0.quote: I take risks I can recover from. Putting my savings into something I don't understand isn't one of them.
fieldNote: She sees risk through a **farm** lens: take what you can recover from, as her father does with cows.
Her farm app already **pays off** for the family, which grounds her calm.

steps.text: Ask the bakery to pay a monthly fee for the forecasting tool
Apply to ten applied-software firms from March
Sign up two more bakeries through the owner's contacts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity, and people should get on board early. I'd tell friends that the tools reward people who start now. I'd say, if you're nervous, pick one small thing to build and do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm pretty comfortable. Entry-level coding jobs will shrink, but I'm learning how to make AI do practical things for real businesses, which is the work that's growing. My pass degree is a drawback on paper, but the bakery tool and the farm app are proof I can ship. I'd keep an eye on how many juniors the bigger firms still take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, turn the bakery tool into a small subscription service and look for ten shops to use it. I'd take a part-time job at a firm that builds business tools, to learn how they do customer support. I'd invest a small part of my savings in the business, like laptops and hosting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, a bit giddy. I like it when the ground moves, as long as I have my boots on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own work would the tools take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tools would write most of my code and the boring parts of reports. That means I'd spend my days on what the customer needs, which is the part I like. I'd also need to be careful and check what the tools produce, since a wrong forecast means bakeries throw away bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to keep farming and to try the new tools slowly. Dad would say machines have always changed farming, and Mum would ask if I'm eating. I'd put a tool on the farm's computer for the milk records, and leave it for them to try.

say: It's a big opportunity, and people should get on board **early**.
If you're nervous, pick **one small thing** to build and do it.
think: Entry coding jobs shrink, but **practical AI for businesses** is growing.
The bakery tool and farm app **prove** I can ship, despite my pass degree.
do: Turn the bakery tool into a **subscription** and look for ten shops.
Take a part-time job at a **business tools** firm to learn support.
feel: Good, a bit giddy: I like the ground moving as long as I have my **boots on**.
S1.quote: I like it when the ground moves, as long as I have my boots on.
fieldNote: Her adaptability turns the scenario into a **business plan**: subscription, shops, part-time work.
Mentions checking **tool output** carefully, since a wrong forecast means wasted bread.

steps.text: Turn the bakery tool into a subscription and find ten shops
Take a part-time job at a business software firm
Spend savings on laptops and hosting for the business
Put a record-keeping tool on the family farm's computer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and I'd be honest that I don't know what comes next. I'd tell friends to look after their families and not to panic-buy anything. At church I'd say we should plan ahead for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious. AI doing any thinking work in two years means my bakery tool could be built by anyone in an afternoon. The robots come by 2031, and a dairy farm needs hands, so my parents have three more years than most, but the farm's prices and loans would change fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, and push the bakery tool to as many shops as possible right away, since the first mover has a few months. I'd keep my savings in cash, and I'd go home on weekends to help my dad think about robot milking. I'd move toward work with a person in it, like running the business, not coding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady in a way. I'd pray, I'd lean on my family, and I'd keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your parents' farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm survives longer than my own job, because robots arrive later. But robot milking and automatic feeders are expensive, and the bank would be nervous. Dad would take on debt, and I'd worry about the milk price in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your choir friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I'm scared too, but I'd rather be scared with people than alone. I'd ask them to come to my place for dinner once a week, so we can talk about it. Singing together helps, I think, more than we'd admit.

say: This is **huge**, and I'd be honest that I don't know what comes next.
At church I'd say we should **plan ahead** for each other.
think: Anyone could build my **bakery tool** in an afternoon.
My parents' farm has about **three more years** than most, but the loans would change fast.
do: Push the bakery tool to as many shops as possible while I'm the **first mover**.
Go home on weekends to help Dad think through **robot milking**.
feel: Anxious but steady: I'd **pray**, lean on family and keep working.
S2.quote: I'd rather be scared with people than alone.
fieldNote: Her adaptability shows as **speed**: she races to sign bakery customers while her edge lasts.
Her answer to fear is **community**: weekly dinners, choir and church.

steps.text: Sign as many bakeries as possible in the first six months
Help Dad compare quotes for robot milking
Hold savings in cash until prices settle
Host a weekly dinner for choir friends to talk it through

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to use well if people are sensible. I'd tell friends to get a skill, save money and not rely on one employer. At church I'd say we should start helping each other early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but hopeful. I'd have three years of building a business before the thinking AI arrives, and some savings and customers. The robots around 2034 would make the farm a hard decision for my parents, but I'd have room to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, grow the bakery tool to a proper product and save a third of my income. I'd keep learning each new tool as it comes. I'd also start a small business in farm software, since I know the work, and I'd partner with my friend Hanna, who's good at sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. It's like standing at a gate, and I can see that the field behind it is bigger than I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd rush and probably get it wrong. With five I can build something solid. I'd test it on real farms and learn who pays. I'd choose customers carefully, and I'd pick the ones who like the product, not just the cheap ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to keep farming and not to borrow for robots until prices fall. We'd write down what each machine costs and how many years it takes to pay back. I'd help with the sums, and if the robots come, we'd be ready for them rather than surprised by them.

say: Five years is enough to **use well** if people are sensible.
I'd tell friends to get a skill, save money and not rely on **one employer**.
think: I'd have three years to build a **business** before the thinking AI arrives.
Robots around 2034 make the farm a **hard decision** for my parents.

Start a **farm software** business with my friend Hanna.
feel: Uneasy but hopeful, like standing at a **gate** and seeing a bigger field.
S3.quote: With two years I'd rush and probably get it wrong. With five I can build something solid.
fieldNote: Time shifts her from **racing** to building something solid, tested on real farms.

steps.text: Turn the bakery tool into a proper product and save a third of income
Start a farm software business with friend Hanna
Work out machine payback years with my parents
Learn each new AI tool as it arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and people should use it kindly and sensibly. I'd tell friends not to wait for someone to tell them what to do. At church I'd say we have time to be generous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. By 2036 I'd be thirty-four, with a business or two, a husband and children perhaps, and enough saved to be flexible. Robots arrive in 2039, and I'd have time to adapt the farm and the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work for a small firm for two years, then go full-time on my own farm software company. I'd save steadily, marry, and start a family around 2031. I'd use every new tool for the business and keep one day a week for family and choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and glad. It feels like a long summer to plant in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the savings and the first customers first, because I can't take risks without a cushion. Then I'd build the company slowly, with real farms paying for it. I wouldn't take investor money early, since I'd like to keep the say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope for in your own family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope for a husband who laughs, two or three children, and a farm still in the family, even if a robot does the milking. I'd like my children to know how to sing, how to cook and how to run a business.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, so use it kindly and sensibly.
I'd tell friends not to wait for **someone to tell them** what to do.
think: By 2036 I'd have a **business or two**, maybe children and savings to be flexible.
Robots arrive in 2039, and I'd have **time** to adapt the farm and the business.
do: Work two years at a small firm, then go **full-time** on my farm software company.
Save steadily, marry and start a **family** around 2031.
feel: Calm and glad, like a long **summer** to plant in.
S4.quote: I hope for a husband who laughs, two or three children, and a farm still in the family, even if a robot does the milking.
fieldNote: With a decade her **business and family plans** fit together, with a firm date for children.

steps.text: Work two years at a small firm, then run my own company

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. My edge as someone who uses the tools would vanish quickly, and my parents' loans would change before they could plan. What would help is time to build things, honest information, and a community that stays together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say this. I use these tools every day, and I'm not the winner by default. I just happen to find it fun, and I know that isn't everyone.

headlineQuote: I use these tools every day, and I'm not the winner by default. I just happen to find it fun, and I know that isn't everyone.
portrait: Kira is a **24-year-old** applied AI master's student with a pass degree, no debt and a dairy farm in her family.
She uses AI **every day** and built a farm app for her parents and a forecasting tool for a bakery.
She is traditional and adaptive: **faith, family** and choir sit beside an appetite for business risk.
Her mood is calm in most worlds, and **anxious** when AGI arrives in two years.
She responds to change by building small **businesses**, signing customers and leaning on her community.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because her edge would vanish fast and her parents' loans would change before they could plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Time** to build things, honest information and a community that stays together.
